items.title: Thanksgiving week weather: Potent coastal storms, rain and snow to impact travel
items.summary:
Thanksgiving week weather: Potent coastal storms, rain and snow to impact travel 

An aerial view of a car driving on a winding mountain road inside a colorful autumn forest. (stock image) (Image credit: rusm/Getty Images) 

November 24, 2026 

As millions of Americans hit the roads, rails and skies to celebrate Turkey Day, the weather will likely bring major holiday headaches to both sides of the country. A powerful coastal storm will lash the eastern half of the nation as a Pacific system brings rain and mountain snow to the West. 

Here’s your Thanksgiving week forecast from NOAA’s Weather Prediction Center :

Wednesday: Storms on the horizon A developing autumn storm will bring scattered showers and a few thunderstorms across the lower Mississippi Valley and Southeast for the busy pre-Thanksgiving travel day. Later Wednesday into Thursday morning, chillier air will wrap into the mid-Mississippi Valley, bringing the chance for some significant wet snow around the St. Louis metro area and the surrounding region.

In the West, a Pacific system will approach the coast and bring the chance for showers to the Pacific Northwest and Northern California. Coastal flooding will also be likely along the West Coast during high tides.

Thursday, Thanksgiving Day: Very windy and rainy for some A potent Thanksgiving Day storm will bring the threat for heavy rain, high winds and flooding spanning the Ohio Valley to the Eastern Seaboard. Strong winds, heavy downpours and coastal flooding will likely impact Thursday morning travel, Turkey Trots and Thanksgiving Day parades from the…
items.t: Thanksgiving week weather: Potent coastal storms, rain and snow to impact travel

items.title: Hurricane season wrap-up: El Nino fueled record number of Pacific storms but calmed Atlantic
items.summary:
Hurricane season wrap-up: El Nino fueled record number of Pacific storms but calmed Atlantic 

November 24, 2026 

A NOAA satellite view of the eye of Hurricane Isaias approaching the U.S. Gulf coast in daytime on October 9, 2026. (Image credit: NOAA Satellites) 

Download Image 

The 2026 hurricane season, which officially ends November 30, will be remembered as a year of contrasts between the Atlantic and Pacific, a classic indication of a hurricane season influenced by a very strong El Nino. Below normal activity across the Atlantic basin was offset by above-average activity in the Pacific, including two disasters in Hawaii.

“NOAA’s unparalleled forecasting skill and scientific expertise provided the early warnings needed to protect lives and property this hurricane season,” said Neil Jacobs, Ph.D., NOAA administrator. “This included accurately predicting this year’s very strong El Nino months in advance, which gave us the critical insight we needed to accurately forecast this season.” 

Atlantic basin The Atlantic basin produced 10 named storms , of which one (Isaias) became a hurricane. Isaias was also the season’s only major hurricane with top sustained winds of 120 mph. An average season has 14 named storms (winds of 39 mph or greater), seven hurricanes (winds of 74 mph or greater), and three major hurricanes (winds of 111 mph or greater).

Tropical Storm Arthur kicked off the season, forming near the Texas coast on June 17, which is close to the average date for the first named storm of the Atlantic season to develop. Though it was a short-lived tropical storm,…
items.t: Hurricane season wrap-up: El Nino fueled record number of Pacific storms but calmed Atlantic
